conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I know the postpartum weeks can feel like a whirlwind of feedings, sleepless nights, and big feelings, and I’m here to help you sort through them with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS.

The EPDS is a quick, 10-question check-in that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up during this huge life change. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, so please feel comfortable answering openly—there are no right or wrong answers, and many new mothers find this first step a relief.

We’ll go through each question one at a time. I’ll ask them conversationally, and you can answer however feels easiest for you—just a sentence or two is perfect. When we’re finished, we’ll look at what your responses tell us and talk about next steps together, if any are needed.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can still laugh, but it’s… muffled, I guess? Like, if my husband shows me a silly meme, I’ll smile—maybe even let out a quick laugh—but the light feeling never lasts. It’s almost immediately followed by this heaviness, like I’m not really allowed to enjoy anything right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not most of the time. I can still laugh a little, but I have to really force it, and the joy fades right away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the next feeding or diaper change. Every so often I’ll think “maybe tomorrow will feel better,” but the actual looking-forward feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I know logically that babies cry, but I still feel like it’s my fault, especially when my husband looks tired or the house is a mess.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot. Even when the baby’s sleeping soundly, I’ll suddenly think, “What if he stops breathing?” or I’ll replay tiny things—like whether I sterilized the bottle right—over and over. There’s this tight, buzzing feeling in my chest most of the day, even when nothing’s actually happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Nothing dramatic—no full panic attacks—but I’ll get this sudden rush of dread, like something bad is about to happen, and my heart races. It passes in a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days. I feel like I’m drowning in small tasks—one feeding ends and the next is already looming, laundry piles up, and I can’t remember if I ate. I keep telling myself “just get through the next hour,” but the sense of being overwhelmed keeps resetting every time I tick one thing off.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up—did I burp him long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and then I’m wide awake. Even when I do drift off, I wake up a couple times with my heart pounding for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that just parks itself over me. I’ll look at the baby and feel this rush of love, but then the sadness creeps back in and I can’t shake it. Some mornings I wake up already feeling heavy, before anything’s even happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah. Not every single day, but probably twice this week. Yesterday it was just because the baby wouldn’t nap and I couldn’t figure out why—tears started rolling and I couldn’t stop them. It feels like the sadness just spills out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…It has. Just quick flashes—like when I’m rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and everything feels hopeless—my mind will throw out, “What if I just disappeared?” I haven’t planned anything and I know I’d never leave him, but the thought pops in once or twice and scares me.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤ 12 mo) – self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

**A. Endorsed Symptoms / Concerns**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, joylessness  
- Daily tearfulness; crying spells triggered by minor stressors  
- Marked loss of interest/anticipation for previously pleasurable activities  
- Pervasive guilt / self-blame regarding parenting competence  
- Heightened, ill-defined anxiety and worry (somatic tension, intrusive “what-if” thoughts)  
- Recurrent, brief panic-like surges (palpitations, dread) without clear precipitant  
- Overwhelmed/drowning feeling with routine infant care/tasks  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry  
- Passive self-harm ideation (“What if I just disappeared”) without plan or intent  

**B. Pattern Summary**  
Consistent with significant depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging post-delivery; functional impairment evident (self-care, household tasks, emotional availability).  

**C. Screening Red Flags**  
- Passive suicidal thoughts present → immediate safety assessment indicated  
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, guilt, and anxiety suggest moderate–severe symptom load  
- Sleep disruption and coping deficits elevate risk for worsening mood and functioning  

**D. Clinical Impression (Screening Level)**  
Findings exceed threshold for routine postpartum mood surveillance; probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety. Recommend prompt comprehensive mental-health evaluation, safety planning, and supportive services.
